item.text:
**3B.1 Research Note**
**Working verdict:** mixed, leaning **no**. I found some procedural respect for electoral institutions and public-language support for open criticism, but the stronger 2024 record is still red-tagging, disinformation, blocked sites, and intimidation of critics. I did **not** find a direct 2024 Marcos statement explicitly affirming alternation of power or conceding that opposition could win in a genuinely open contest.

| Direction | Claim-level item | Source | Date | URL | QIDs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Positive | Marcos told critics to let Comelec handle allegations that signatures in the people’s initiative drive may have been bought. That is a small but real sign of deference to the election body rather than direct executive interference. | GMA News Online | 2024-01-23 | https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/895067/marcos-on-people-s-initiative-for-cha-cha-let-comelec-do-their-job/story/ | 4B.1 |
| Positive | Marcos publicly pledged a free and safe environment for journalists and said critical press is better than cooperative press. That supports a toleration of contestation in the public sphere that elections depend on. | Presidential Communications Office | 2024-04-15 | https://pco.gov.ph/news_releases/pbbm-declares-free-safe-environment-for-journalists-under-bagong-pilipinas/ | 4B.1, 3B.3, 3B.8 |
| Mixed | Freedom House says Philippine elections are free from overt restrictions, but not fully fair because disinformation and vote buying distort competition; it also says red-tagging persisted under Marcos. This is the strongest broad outside assessment, but it is not a clean endorsement of Marcos’s own commitment. | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/philippines/freedom-world/2024 | 4B.1, 3B.3, 3B.8 |
| Negative | HRW said red-tagging under Marcos placed leftist activists and critics at serious risk, with officials and supporters accusing them of communist ties. That is inconsistent with a ruler who genuinely accepts competitive politics. | Human Rights Watch | 2024-01-11 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/philippines-red-tagging-puts-activists-risk | 4B.1, 3B.3, 3B.8 |
| Negative | Amnesty says Marcos-era actors weaponized digital tools, misinformation, and the anti-terror law to create fear, and that red-tagging vilified activists, journalists, teachers, and others. That undercuts meaningful electoral contestability. | Amnesty International | 2024-10-14 | https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa35/8574/2024/en/ | 4B.1, 3B.3, 3B.8 |
| Negative | The Reuters Institute report says red-tagging, libel pressure, blocked sites, and threats against journalists persisted under Marcos. This points to a coercive information environment that weakens free and fair competition. | Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism | 2024-06-17 | https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2024/philippines | 4B.1, 3B.3, 3B.8 |
| Negative | HRW’s 2025 report on 2024 says extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and political violence persisted, with violence against local officials increasing ahead of the 2025 midterms. That suggests elections were still embedded in a coercive political order. | Human Rights Watch | 2025-01-16 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/philippines | 4B.1, 3B.10, 3B.8 |

**Bottom line:** Marcos showed some procedural respect for institutions, but the broader 2024 environment still featured intimidation and information manipulation that are hard to reconcile with a genuine acceptance that power should be contestable through free, fair, and meaningful elections.

**Search gap:** I did not find a direct 2024 Marcos statement explicitly endorsing alternation of power, accepting a possible future defeat, or committing to a fully neutral electoral playing field. The best evidence is indirect and mostly about the surrounding civic environment.
